Temple Tax
TEM-puhl taks
noun
The half-shekel paid by every Israelite for the service of the sanctuary; in the Gospels, the tribute money of Matthew 17.

📖 Biblical Definition

The temple tax was the half-shekel required of every Israelite male for the service and upkeep of the sanctuary, rooted in the atonement money of Exodus, where every man numbered gave a ransom for his soul, the rich no more and the poor no less than half a shekel, a memorial before the LORD. In the Gospel of Matthew, those who received this tribute money asked Peter whether his Master paid it; and the Lord taught Peter a deep lesson by a question: of whom do the kings of the earth take custom, of their own children, or of strangers? Peter answered, Of strangers; and Jesus said, Then are the children free—for He, the Son of the God whose house the temple was, owed no tax for His Father’s house. Yet lest they should offend, He bade Peter cast a hook into the sea, and in the mouth of the first fish was found a coin sufficient to pay for them both. The scene reveals both the dignity of the Son, free in His Father’s house, and His gracious condescension, paying what He did not owe, and His sovereign provision drawn even from the sea. The dictionary honors the temple tax narrative as a window into the Sonship of Christ, His voluntary humility, and the lordship by which He provides for His own.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The half-shekel for the sanctuary; in Matthew 17, Christ, the free Son, yet paid it lest He offend, providing the coin from the mouth of a fish.

TEMPLE TAX, the half-shekel required of every Israelite for the sanctuary.

Rooted in the atonement money of Exodus, a ransom for the soul.

In Matthew 17, asked whether Jesus paid the tribute money.

The Son is free in His Father’s house, yet paid lest He offend.

The coin was found in the mouth of the first fish (Mat 17:27).

📖 Key Scripture

Mat 17:26 — "Peter saith unto him, Of strangers. Jesus saith unto him, Then are the children free."

Mat 17:27 — "Notwithstanding, lest we should offend them, go thou to the sea, and cast an hook, and take up the fish that first cometh up; and when thou hast opened his mouth, thou shalt find a piece of money: that take, and give unto them for me and thee."

Exo 30:13 — "This they shall give, every one that passeth among them that are numbered, half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary: (a shekel is twenty gerahs:) an half shekel shall be the offering of the LORD."

2Co 8:9 — "For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The episode is treated as a mere wonder-tale or a lesson in civic duty; it reveals the Sonship, condescension, and sovereign provision of Christ.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the flattening of the scene into either a quaint wonder-tale about a coin in a fish or a bare lesson in paying one’s dues. Both miss the weight of the Lord’s teaching. The point turns on Sonship: the children of the king are free from His tribute, and Jesus, the Son of the God whose house the temple was, owed nothing for His Father’s house (Matt 17:26). The episode is first a revelation of who He is.

The principle to recover is the union of Christ’s dignity, His condescension, and His provision. Though free, He paid the tax lest He should offend (Matt 17:27), foreshadowing the deeper grace by which, though He was rich, for our sakes He became poor (2 Cor 8:9), paying a debt He did not owe. And He provided the very coin by His sovereign lordship, drawing it from the mouth of a fish in the sea—a small parable of the Lord who owns the cattle on a thousand hills and provides for His own from sources no man foresees. The humble half-shekel becomes a window into the Son who stoops and the Lord who supplies.
